# Exoplanet 51 Peg b

<a class="gallery-back" href="../gallery.qmd">← Back to Gallery</a>

**Topic:** Lomb–Scargle periodogram for unevenly sampled astronomical time series.
**Chapter:** [2 — Frequency Domain](../chap2.qmd)

---

## Background

51 Pegasi b was the first exoplanet confirmed around a Sun-like star (Mayor & Queloz, 1995). It was detected via the **radial-velocity method**: the planet's gravity causes the host star to wobble, Doppler-shifting its spectral lines periodically. Observations from ground-based telescopes are necessarily sparse and irregular — the DFT requires uniformly sampled data, but the Lomb–Scargle periodogram handles arbitrary sampling gaps.

The orbital period is 4.23 days, corresponding to a frequency of ~0.236 day⁻¹.

## Key idea

For an unevenly sampled dataset $\{(t_i, x_i)\}$, the Lomb–Scargle periodogram is defined as

$$
P(\omega) = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left[
  \frac{\left(\sum_i x_i \cos\omega(t_i - \tau)\right)^2}{\sum_i \cos^2\omega(t_i - \tau)}
  +
  \frac{\left(\sum_i x_i \sin\omega(t_i - \tau)\right)^2}{\sum_i \sin^2\omega(t_i - \tau)}
\right]
$$

where $\tau$ is chosen to make the two terms statistically independent. The false-alarm probability quantifies how likely a peak of given height is under the null hypothesis of pure noise.

## Code

```python
import numpy as np
from astropy.timeseries import LombScargle
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load 51 Peg radial-velocity measurements
# Columns: BJD, RV (m/s), uncertainty (m/s)
data = np.loadtxt('docs/Data/UID_0113357_RVC_001.tbl.txt', comments='#')
t, rv, rv_err = data[:, 0], data[:, 1], data[:, 2]

# Normalise to zero mean
rv -= rv.mean()

# Lomb-Scargle
ls = LombScargle(t, rv, rv_err)
freq, power = ls.autopower(minimum_frequency=0.05,
                            maximum_frequency=2.0,
                            samples_per_peak=10)

# False-alarm levels
fap_levels = [0.1, 0.01, 0.001]
fap_powers = [ls.false_alarm_level(fap) for fap in fap_levels]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 6))

# Data
axes[0].errorbar(t % 4.23, rv, yerr=rv_err, fmt='o', ms=3, lw=0.8,
                 label='phase-folded at 4.23 d')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Phase (days)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('RV (m/s)')

# Periodogram
axes[1].plot(1.0 / freq, power, lw=0.9)
for fap, pwr in zip(fap_levels, fap_powers):
    axes[1].axhline(pwr, ls='--', lw=0.8, label=f'FAP = {fap}')
axes[1].axvline(4.23, color='C1', lw=1.5, label='P = 4.23 d')
axes[1].set_xscale('log')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Period (days)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Lomb–Scargle power')
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)

plt.tight_layout()
```

## Result

<div class="gallery-result">
![Lomb–Scargle periodogram of 51 Peg b radial-velocity data showing peak at 4.23 days](../Figure/figure_lombscargle_51Pegasib.png)
</div>

The periodogram shows an overwhelming peak at a period of 4.23 days, far above all three false-alarm thresholds. No other significant peaks are present, confirming a single-planet system with a 4.23-day orbital period.
